title: Kaitai Shinsho: Dutch anatomy in Japan

confidence.note: The printed book is dated 1774 and survives in library collections; the 1771 dissection and the struggle to translate are known chiefly from Sugita Genpaku's memoir, written decades later in 1815, so its vivid details are one participant's recollection.

people: Maeno Ryōtaku (1723–1803), physician and, with Sugita, one of the two core translators
Johann Adam Kulmus (1689–1745), German author of the original anatomy
summary: Japanese doctors took a Dutch anatomy book to a dissection, marveled at its accuracy, and spent three and a half years translating it, shaking the authority of Chinese anatomy.
body: In 1771 the Edo physicians Sugita Genpaku, Maeno Ryōtaku and Nakagawa Jun'an watched the dissection of an executed convict at the Kozukappara execution ground, carrying a Dutch book, *Ontleedkundige Tafelen* (1734), itself a translation of Johann Adam Kulmus's German anatomy tables. They were amazed at how accurately it matched the body. With little Dutch between them, they spent three and a half years and eleven revisions translating it. *Kaitai Shinsho* ("New Book of Anatomy") appeared in 1774, written in *kanbun*, a style using only classical Chinese characters, and it called into question the Chinese anatomical theory taught in Japan's *kanpō* medicine.

links.note: Kulmus's plates were imitations of a lineage of illustration patterned on Vesalius.
A generation later, Hanaoka joined Chinese medicine to Dutch-style surgery.

title: Hanaoka Seishū operates under general anesthesia

confidence.note: The operation is recorded by Hanaoka's own school and later Japanese histories, and surgical historians accept it as the earliest well-documented general anesthesia; accounts differ on whether it was a lumpectomy or a partial mastectomy. Japanese sources give the day as 13 October of Bunka 1 (1804); because Japan then used a lunisolar calendar, a conversion to the Western calendar could shift it, and none of the accounts consulted says whether that was done. Older Chinese stories of surgical anesthetics, such as Hua Tuo's, are tradition rather than record.

people: Hanaoka Seishū (1760–1835), surgeon who devised the anesthetic *mafutsusan*
Kamada Gendai, his pupil, who published a textbook on the method c. 1840
summary: In 1804 a Japanese surgeon put a woman to sleep with an herbal brew and removed her breast tumor, four decades before ether; why the world never heard of it is still argued.
body: On 13 October 1804, in Wakayama, Japan, the surgeon Hanaoka Seishū gave a 60-year-old woman with breast cancer an herbal drink of his own devising, *mafutsusan*, and removed her tumor while she lay unconscious. It is the earliest well-documented operation under general anesthesia, nearly four decades before Crawford Long used ether in Georgia in 1842. Today it is often called *tsūsensan*, but Hanaoka and his pupils wrote *mafutsusan*; the other name appears in Edo-period documents only on his epitaph.

Hanaoka (1760–1835) had studied Chinese medicine in Kyoto alongside Dutch surgical techniques, and knew of Hua Tuo's legendary anesthetic. His mixture was built on datura, whose alkaloids scopolamine and atropine sedate and blur memory, together with aconite. He worked on it for years, trying it on dogs and then on his wife and mother, and went on to remove more than 150 breast cancers.

Why did it not spread abroad? The drug was toxic and hard to dose, and Japan was nearly closed to outsiders. Popular accounts add that Hanaoka kept the formula secret, but historians of Japanese anesthesia dispute that: he taught openly, and his pupil Kamada Gendai published a textbook around 1840. Disciples were, however, sternly asked not to leak the recipe, which one printed in 1862.

links.note: Hanaoka set out to recreate the anesthetic attributed to Hua Tuo.

title: 'Traditional Chinese Medicine' is assembled

confidence.note: The policy turns, the Academy of 1955 and the training courses are documented, and a peer-reviewed health-policy review says Mao authorized a systematized medicine in the 1950s. How far the result was new rather than a continuation is a matter of emphasis: Republican-era reformers had already begun to modernize Chinese medicine, and the sharpest 'Mao invented it' framing comes from critics rather than all historians.

summary: The textbook 'traditional Chinese medicine' was built in the 1950s, when the Communist state turned varied older practices into one teachable system of colleges, courses and standard theory.
body: By 1955 China had about 70,000 Western-trained doctors and 360,000 Chinese-medicine practitioners, working from highly varied lineages and texts. Mao Zedong's government set out to make a system of them: first pressing practitioners to 'scientize', then in 1954 telling Western-trained doctors to study Chinese medicine instead. An Academy of Traditional Chinese Medicine was founded in 1955, Ministry of Health courses of about two and a half years taught Western-trained scientists such as Tu Youyou Chinese medicine from the late 1950s, and theory, herbal prescribing and acupuncture points were standardized.

myth.tradition: Traditional Chinese Medicine is a single system handed down unchanged for thousands of years.
myth.record: Its standard theory, textbooks and institutions were assembled under the state in the 1950s, building on Republican-era reform efforts and drawing selectively on much older and more varied traditions.

links.note: The rural health drive that put herbal and Western medicine in the same hands.

title: The barefoot doctors

confidence.note: Mao's 1965 criticism, the official title in 1968 and the 1985 renaming are well documented; village health workers had precursors in the 1950s and in commune health stations from 1958, so the start date is a convention. Its achievements are harder to judge: many claims of success were not backed by data, and falls in infectious disease cannot be credited to barefoot doctors alone.

summary: Peasants with a few months' training brought vaccines, first aid and acupuncture to China's villages, and the program was studied abroad as a model for rural primary care.
body: In 1965 Mao Zedong complained that health care served the cities, home to about 15 percent of the population, while the peasant majority had almost no access to doctors or medicine. "In health and medical work," he ordered, "put the stress on rural areas." Urban medical teams went to the villages, and young peasants, mostly in their twenties with some schooling, received three to six months of training in anatomy, diagnosis, acupuncture, herbal and Western drugs, birth control and maternal care. They kept farming, gave vaccinations and first aid, taught hygiene and referred harder cases to commune health centers. Grassroots health workers had been trained in some places since the 1950s, and the name 'barefoot doctors' became official in 1968.

Abroad they became a legend: In the 1970s WHO and several developing countries studied it as a cheap alternative to Western-style care, and one review says it greatly influenced the 1978 Alma-Ata Declaration. At home the record is mixed. Claims of success were often unsupported by data, some barefoot doctors treated complicated illnesses beyond their training, and the cities lost doctors, yet China did cut infectious diseases such as schistosomiasis sharply. In the 1980s state support shrank and farmers paid for care; in 1985 the title gave way to 'rural doctor'.

links.note: WHO looked to China's program as a model while primary health care was being defined.

title: Artemisinin: an old text and a new drug

confidence.note: The laboratory dates come from Tu Youyou's own detailed 2015 account and the Nobel Committee's review, and are not seriously contested. What is contested is credit: Project 523 was a large, secret, collective program, and historians working from newly published Chinese records argue that crediting one person oversimplifies it.

people: Tu Youyou (b. 1930), pharmacologist who led the Project 523 group at the Institute of Chinese Materia Medica
Ge Hong (284–363), physician and author of the *Handbook of Prescriptions for Emergencies*
summary: A secret wartime project, a fourth-century recipe and a cold-extraction trick produced artemisinin, now the backbone of malaria treatment worldwide.
body: In January 1969 Tu Youyou, a pharmacologist at Beijing's Institute of Chinese Materia Medica, was made head of a research group in Project 523, a secret military program named for a secret meeting that opened in Beijing on 23 May 1967. The need was urgent. Malaria was crippling soldiers on both sides of the Vietnam War, drug-resistant parasites had spread, and several thousand compounds screened in China since 1967 had failed. Tu's group was told to search among Chinese remedies, in the middle of the Cultural Revolution, when most research had stopped.

Her team gathered some 2,000 recipes, condensed them into 640 prescriptions and tested extracts of more than a hundred herbs on infected rodents. Qinghao, sweet wormwood (*Artemisia annua*), looked promising but gave erratic results. Tu then noticed a line in Ge Hong's *Handbook of Prescriptions for Emergencies*, written around 340 CE: "A handful of qinghao immersed in two liters of water, wring out the juice and drink it all." Soaked, not boiled. Suspecting that heat was destroying the active ingredient, she switched to low-temperature extraction with ether. On 4 October 1971 sample no. 191 inhibited the parasites in rodents completely. In July 1972 Tu and two colleagues swallowed the extract to test its safety; that autumn it cured all 21 patients treated on Hainan Island; and in November 1972 the team isolated the active crystals, later named *qinghaosu*, artemisinin.

The molecule contained no nitrogen and belonged to a new class of antimalarials, chemically unlike quinine, that kills the parasite fast. Adoption abroad was slow. Chinese scientists presented their work to a WHO meeting in Beijing in 1981, but WHO's endorsement of artemisinin-based combination therapy came much later (one history dates it to 2005), after resistance to older drugs had become widespread. Combinations are used partly to slow resistance, which has now emerged in some parts of the world.

Tu shared the 2015 Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine. The single name sits uneasily on a collective effort: after she reported her results at a project meeting in March 1972, research teams across China took up qinghao, and the molecule's structure was worked out with chemists at the Shanghai Institute of Organic Chemistry and the Institute of Biophysics. Nor is artemisinin simply an ancient remedy rediscovered. Ge Hong supplied a clue; solvents, chromatography and clinical trials made the drug.

myth.tradition: Artemisinin is a traditional Chinese herbal cure, rediscovered single-handedly by Tu Youyou.
myth.record: Ge Hong's fourth-century recipe gave a vital hint about cold extraction, but the drug is a purified compound isolated with modern chemistry in 1971–72, inside a large state program in which many teams took part.

links.note: Ge Hong's soaking recipe for qinghao suggested extracting without heat.
